newsitem.title: SENEGAL: Guinea-Bissau move to CFA franc deemed successful.
newsitem.headline: Guinea-Bissau move to CFA franc deemed successful.

text.p: The impoverished West African state of Guinea-Bissau became a full member of the Franc Zone on Friday when the CFA franc replaced the peso as its currency.
The two currencies have been circulating in tandem since May, when Guinea-Bissau joined the West African Monetary Union (UMOA), which forms one half of the Zone in Africa.
The deputy general manager of what was Guinea-Bissau's central bank told Reuters by telephone that pesos were no longer in circulation.
"The operation to replace the peso with the CFA franc has been 97 percent successful, according to our provisional results," Hugo Bores said.
"Clearly, we can expect to get even higher figures. It's a total success, more than we hoped for," he added.
The central bank is now a national office of UMOA's central bank, the BCEAO, which is based in Dakar, Senegal.
The peso has been exchangeable at a rate of 65 to one CFA franc. The CFA franc itself is linked to the French franc, and there are currently around 620 per U.S. dollar.

Guinea-Bissau, a former Portuguese colony, hopes its membership of UMOA and its transfer to what is effectively a hard currency thanks to a French Treasury guarantee will allow it to match the impressive economic growth rates shown by other members, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo.
However, the changeover met with a mixed reaction among the populace, not least because it has been blamed for an increase in inflation in recent weeks.
Earlier this week, a senior BCEAO official denied the currency change was fuelling inflation.
A BCEAO spokesman told Ivory Coast's Fraternite-Matin newspaper that the bank had monitored a basket of 26 goods, and, while some prices had risen, that was mainly due to seasonal factors.

However, he accepted that the exchange rate of 65 pesos for one CFA franc might cause problems for some poorly-educated Guinea-Bissau people, and he said some traders might have taken advantage of the situation to raise prices.
"It's like traders are joking when you ask the price of a food item. The state should regulate the prices, otherwise we won't make it," said one disgruntled shopper.
On the plus side, some people noted that travellers would no longer have the problem of trying to exchange a soft currency, and the business community was cautiously enthusiastic.
"I think it's a good thing, because CFA francs can be changed into another currency. But I am a bit worried about the social impact of this move," businessman Barros Domingos said.
